The answer to when university stopped being free depends on the country and institution in question, as different places ended free higher education at different times.

In the United States, the shift away from free public higher education began in the 1960s [d5][d6]. California's public colleges and universities stopped being tuition-free when Gov. Ronald Reagan cut funding and proposed charging fees in the 1960s, with the transition to student fees in the UC and California State systems beginning shortly after Reagan became governor in 1967 [d6][d9]. The official "no tuition" policy in California's community colleges did not end until 1982 [d9]. More broadly across the US, registration and instructional fees began to be instated around 1959, and full tuition was imposed by 1969 [d3]. Free tuition at the City University of New York (CUNY) came to an end in 1976 [d7].

In Britain, higher education was effectively free between 1962 and the 1990s, as the state paid students' tuition fees and offered maintenance grants following the Anderson committee report [d1]. England's free university system ended around the 1998 reforms [d8].
